stem: Explain why a firm may continue to produce in the short run even though it is making a loss.

points.description: Fixed costs must be paid even if the firm closes.

The loss from producing is therefore less than the loss from closing (the fixed cost).

The firm may also expect the price to recover and want to keep its workers and customers.

stem: Distinguish between profit maximisation and cost minimisation.

points.description: Profit maximisation chooses the output at which TR − TC is greatest (MC = MR).
Cost minimisation chooses the combination of inputs that gives the lowest cost for a given output.
A profit maximiser must also minimise the cost of its chosen output, but a cost minimiser does not necessarily choose the profit-maximising output.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Profit maximisation is about choosing the output (and price) at which total revenue exceeds total cost by the most, where MC = MR. Cost minimisation is about producing a given output at the lowest possible cost, by choosing the best combination of inputs. A profit maximiser must also be a cost minimiser at its chosen output, but a firm that minimises the cost of a fixed output may not have chosen the output that maximises profit.

explanation: Output choice versus input choice.

stem: Assess whether a firm that is making a loss should always close down.

points.description: In the short run fixed costs are paid whether the firm produces or not.
If price is above AVC, producing gives a contribution to fixed cost and a smaller loss than closing.
If price is below AVC, closing is better because producing adds to the loss.
In the long run the firm must cover ATC (including normal profit) or leave.
Expectations: a temporary fall in price may justify staying open; permanent decline does not.
Closing may have costs: loss of skilled workers, customers and contracts, redundancy payments.
A firm with social aims (a state-owned enterprise) may continue at a loss.
A justified judgement.

levels.descriptor: Two-sided, applied and developed, with a justified conclusion.
Some development of one side, limited application or conclusion.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: In the short run a firm has fixed costs to pay whether or not it produces, so a loss is not enough reason to close. If the price is above average variable cost, producing earns a contribution to fixed cost and loses less than closing. If the price is below average variable cost, producing adds to the loss, and the firm should close. In the long run, all costs are variable, so the firm must cover average total cost, including normal profit, or leave. Expectations matter: a temporary fall in price may justify staying open, while a permanent fall does not. Closing may also lose skilled workers and customers, and a state-owned firm may continue at a loss for social reasons. Overall the right decision is to close only when price is below average variable cost in the short run, and to leave the industry when it expects price to stay below average total cost.

explanation: Short-run test: AVC; long-run test: ATC; expectations matter.
hints: Distinguish the short run from the long run.
